frictions.title: When2meet availability schedule lacks accessible grid semantics, keyboard focusability, and slot labels
frictions.description: VoiceOver reads loose time and date labels in sequence, but the availability calendar grid lacks accessible table or grid semantics, cell coordinates, focusable tab stops, and keyboard-operable controls for selecting time slots (WCAG 1.3.1, 2.1.1, 4.1.2).

interventions.description: Add ARIA grid semantics, accessible cell labels, and keyboard navigation to the availability schedule.

The availability schedule on the event page exposes no interactive time-slot elements to assistive technology or the keyboard. VoiceOver traversal reached only static date and time strings (e.g. 'Aug 14', '10:00 AM', 'Aug 15') with no role, selection state, or row/column relationship, so the two-dimensional structure of the schedule (which time belongs to which date) is not programmatically conveyed. Tab navigation bypassed the schedule region completely, moving from surrounding page content to PayPal controls and then browser chrome, meaning there is no focusable tab stop for any slot. Repeated VO+Space activation on the schedule labels produced no state change. Consequence: a keyboard or screen reader user cannot determine or set their availability at all, which is the sole purpose of the page; the observed session ended in task abandonment.
interventions.mitigation: Expose the schedule as a programmatically structured, keyboard-operable widget rather than positioned static text. Give the schedule container an appropriate grid/table role with row and cell roles for the slot elements, and associate the existing date column and time row labels as programmatic headers (or provide an equivalent per-cell accessible name such as 'Friday, August 14, 9:00 AM'). Make slots reachable from the keyboard (a roving tabindex within the grid, or per-cell focusable elements such as buttons or checkboxes), render a visible focus indicator, and bind Enter/Space to toggle availability with arrow-key movement between cells. Expose each slot's current availability as a programmatic state (for example a toggle/selected state) so the change is announced after activation, and verify the schedule appears in the page's focus order instead of being skipped. Where feasible, also offer a non-grid alternative (e.g. per-day time range inputs) as a redundant path to submitting availability.

frictions.title: Unlabeled sign-in text fields missing accessible names in Form Controls Rotor
frictions.description: When exploring form controls via the VoiceOver Rotor, the 'Your Name' and 'Password' text inputs (#name, #password) lack programmatic labels (<label> or aria-label), causing VoiceOver to omit clear accessible names in the Form Controls list (WCAG 1.3.1, 4.1.2).

interventions.description: Add accessible labels to the 'Your Name' and 'Password' input fields so VoiceOver identifies them in the Form Controls menu.

The 'Your Name' and 'Password' text inputs (#name, #password) were observed in the DOM and accessibility tree without an associated <label> or aria-label. When the user opened the VoiceOver Rotor Form Controls menu, these fields were listed without a clear accessible name, so a screen reader user scanning the form controls list cannot tell which field is which, nor that the page offers a sign-in/identification step at all. The barrier recurred across segments, indicating it is a persistent property of the page rather than a transient state.
interventions.mitigation: Associate a programmatic label with each input: add a <label for="name">Your Name</label> and <label for="password">Password</label> pair, or, where visible label markup cannot be changed, set aria-label (e.g. aria-label="Your Name" on #name and aria-label="Password" on #password). Ensure the accessible name matches the visible text next to each field, and verify the names are announced in the VoiceOver Rotor Form Controls list. Where the visible copy indicates the password is optional, reflect that in the label or in programmatically associated help text rather than in placeholder text alone.

frictions.title: Unlabeled link announced as 'link' in VoiceOver Rotor
frictions.description: While traversing links in the VoiceOver Rotor, VoiceOver encounters a link lacking accessible text and announces it merely as 'link', providing no context regarding its destination or purpose (WCAG 2.4.4, 4.1.2).

interventions.description: Provide accessible text for unlabeled links so VoiceOver announces their purpose in the Rotor.

While traversing the VoiceOver Rotor Links menu, an anchor element with no accessible text was announced only as 'link'. In the rotor the link is presented out of its surrounding page context, so the user receives no indication of the link's destination or purpose and cannot decide whether to activate it. This was observed repeatedly across multiple segments of the session.
interventions.mitigation: Give every anchor a non-empty accessible name. If the link's content is an icon or image, supply alt text on the image or an aria-label on the anchor describing the destination or action; if the anchor is a decorative or purely structural element, remove it from the link role rather than exposing an empty link. Audit the page for anchors whose computed accessible name is empty and verify each one is announced with meaningful text in the VoiceOver Rotor Links list.

frictions.title: Carousel buttons present ambiguous accessible name for screen reader
frictions.description: VoiceOver announces 'Visit linked content, button' for multiple consecutive carousel cards because an explicit aria-label attribute overrides the distinct image alt text inside each button, obscuring their actual targets (WCAG 2.4.4, WCAG 4.1.2).

interventions.description: Update carousel item labels to announce each item's specific content description instead of generic text.

Interactive carousel cards on the homepage each expose the same static accessible name. VoiceOver announced 'Visit linked content, button' repeatedly as the person moved through consecutive carousel items with VO-Left, so no announcement distinguished one card's destination from another. Evidence from the page DOM shows the carousel item containers carry an explicit aria-label='Visit linked content', which takes precedence over the more descriptive alt text present on the child img elements (e.g. 'Little Leaders Characters', 'Little Leaders Videos'). The consequence is that a screen reader user cannot determine where any individual card leads without activating it and inspecting the resulting page, which makes carousel navigation guess-and-check and slows or blocks reaching a specific destination.
interventions.mitigation: Give each carousel item a unique, meaningful accessible name that reflects its own destination or content. Either remove the generic aria-label from the item container so accessible name computation falls back to the inner image's alt text, or set the container's aria-label to the item's specific title. Apply the same naming logic to dynamically generated or cloned slides so newly inserted items are not left with the generic label, and verify with VoiceOver that consecutive items announce distinct names while preserving existing focus and hover behaviour.

blind.description: The Elfsight photo-gallery carousel exposes each slide as a generic `div role="button" aria-label="Visit linked content"` (repeated many times because Swiper duplicates slides), so a screen-reader user hears a dozen identical, purpose-less controls with no idea of the destination.

The Elfsight previous/next controls are `div role="button" aria-label="Previous"/"Next"` with no `tabindex`, so they are not focusable and a keyboard/screen-reader user cannot move through that gallery at all.

Both the desktop and mobile header markup (plus the overlay menu) are present in the DOM, so the Shop/Books/Playground/About links, the "Login" link and the "0 items in cart" link are announced two to three times, and the two `background-pause-button` pairs expose both "Pause Background" and "Play Background" simultaneously, creating duplicated, contradictory controls.
The menu toggle button computes the name "Open Menu Close Menu" (both spans read) and carries no `aria-expanded`, so its purpose and open/closed state are not conveyed.

Decorative scrolling marquee phrases are marked up as multiple `<h1>` elements ("Motor Skill Development", "•", "Multi-Lingual Content") and "Why Little Leaders?" is another h1, so heading navigation returns meaningless, duplicated headings instead of a real page structure.

low_vision.description: The marquee block scrolls its heading text continuously along an SVG path with no pause/stop control, making the text impossible to read at magnification.

Two auto-rotating carousels (the Elfsight swiper gallery and the `user-items-list-carousel` with its "Item 1 of 8" live region) change content on their own, so magnified users lose the item they were reading.

Long white bold testimonial text (`sqsrte-text-color--white`) sits directly over a photographic section background (`image-asset.jpg`) with only a translucent overlay, so contrast varies and can fall below 4.5:1.

Headings use Squarespace viewport-scaled text (`sqsrte-scaled-text-container`) and fluid image blocks, so text size is tied to container width rather than user text settings and can clip or fail to enlarge when zoomed/resized.

The transparent sticky header (`tweak-transparent-header`, `tweak-fixed-header-style-scroll-back`) overlays page content and consumes a large share of the viewport at high zoom, obscuring content beneath it.

dhh.description: The embedded Vimeo videos ("Little Leaders Classics Video Series (Official Trailer)" and "Why Little Leaders?") are presented with no indication of captions, so their narration, music and dialogue are inaccessible.

No transcript or text alternative accompanies either video block — the only adjacent text is the credit "A message from our founder, Bradley Silvius" — so the spoken content of the founder's message is unavailable.

motor.description: The Elfsight gallery relies on Swiper drag/swipe plus `div role="button"` arrows that are not in the tab order, leaving no keyboard or single-pointer alternative for browsing its slides.
The marquee's clickable hitbox path and the auto-advancing carousels move continuously, forcing users to hit a moving target with no way to stop the motion first.

Interactive icons are small and thin — the cart icon, the hairline SVG carousel arrows (`user-items-list-carousel__arrow-icon`, 24×14 mobile arrows) and the Elfsight 16×16 arrow icons — making accurate pointer activation difficult.
Footer links are packed inline with only whitespace between them (`Privacy Policy Terms and Conditions`), so adjacent targets are effectively touching and easy to mis-click.

Because both desktop and mobile header blocks plus the overlay menu are all in the DOM, keyboard users must tab through triplicated nav links, "Login" (an inert `href="#"` link) and cart links before reaching content, greatly increasing keystrokes and dead-end activations.

frictions.title: Ambiguous 'Visit linked content' accessible names on gallery buttons
frictions.description: Photo gallery carousel controls use identical aria-label attributes ('Visit linked content'), overriding child image alt text and forcing VoiceOver users to perform trial activations to discover button destinations.

interventions.description: Replace generic 'Visit linked content' button labels with each slide's descriptive title.

If the carousel clones or lazily adds slide nodes, apply the same naming logic when those nodes are created so newly inserted controls are not left with the generic label.

frictions.title: Click CAPTCHA image challenge inaccessible with VoiceOver
frictions.description: The visual Click CAPTCHA requires spatial image inspection and pointing. Interacting with the image and controls via VoiceOver provides no nonvisual representation or accessible alternative, leaving the user unable to solve or verify the CAPTCHA.

interventions.description: The Click CAPTCHA challenge depends entirely on visually locating and pointing at specific regions of an image. When traversed with VoiceOver, the challenge image provided no nonvisual representation of the task or of the selectable regions, and repeated VO-Space activations on the image and on the 'Check' and 'Reset' buttons produced no announced result or state change. Consequently a screen reader user has no way to determine what must be clicked, no way to indicate a selection nonvisually, and no feedback about whether verification succeeded or failed — the CAPTCHA gate, and therefore the flow it protects, is unpassable without sight.
interventions.mitigation: Provide a non-visual alternative for the same security check that is reachable and announced in the accessibility tree (for example an audio challenge or a non-cognitive/non-visual verification path), and expose it as a real focusable control with an accessible name rather than a visual-only affordance. Make each selectable region of the challenge an individually focusable, keyboard-operable element with a descriptive accessible name and a programmatic selected state, so selection does not require pointer targeting of image coordinates. Announce verification outcome (success, failure, remaining attempts) through a live region or an equivalent status mechanism so the result of activating 'Check' and 'Reset' is perceivable without vision. Where feasible, prefer a verification method that does not require the user to solve a visual puzzle at all.

Body and helper text uses light grays on light or dark grounds (`text-steel-gray` on white, `text-silver-blue` on `bg-charcoal-blue`, 12px labels) that are likely below 4.5:1 contrast.

frictions.title: Unannounced product availability update on size selection
frictions.description: Selecting the XS size radio button visually changes product status to 'Sold Out' and displays an out-of-stock form, but VoiceOver receives no live region announcement or status update conveying this change (WCAG 4.1.3).

interventions.description: Announce product stock availability changes to screen reader users when selecting size options.

Activating the XS size radio button updates the DOM to reflect an unavailable variant: a 'variant--soldout' class is applied, the submit button label changes to 'Sold Out', and a Klaviyo back-in-stock email form is revealed. None of this is conveyed programmatically as a status update, so VoiceOver announced only 'XS' and 'selectable text'. The user continued arrowing to adjacent size options unaware that the availability state and the purchase control had changed, and only encountered the newly revealed email form incidentally through sequential navigation. Screen reader users can therefore misread the page state, attempt to purchase an unavailable variant, or miss the back-in-stock alternative entirely.
interventions.mitigation: Add a polite live status region within the product form container and update it whenever a size radio changes, so the resulting availability state is announced (for example, 'XS — sold out. Notify me when back in stock form available.'). Derive the announcement text from the same availability state that drives the visual change (the sold-out class / submit button text) so the two cannot diverge, guard against duplicate or repeated speech when the same variant is re-selected, and ensure the change in the submit control's accessible name and disabled state is exposed programmatically. Because the newly revealed email form is additional content, also make its presence discoverable to assistive technology at the moment it appears rather than only via sequential traversal.

frictions.title: Sold-out XS size radio button missing disabled accessible state
frictions.description: The XS size radio button visually displays sold-out styling, but its HTML input element lacks disabled or aria-disabled attributes. VoiceOver announces it as an active radio button, leading the user to select an unavailable option without prior warning.

interventions.description: Expose sold-out size options as disabled to VoiceOver.

The XS size option on the product page is presented as sold out purely through visual styling (sold-out class, strikethrough text), while its radio input exposes no disabled or aria-disabled state and no sold-out wording in its accessible name. VoiceOver therefore announced it as 'XS radio button, 2 of 10', identical to purchasable sizes, and the user selected an unavailable variant. The resulting out-of-stock change in the purchase area was not announced either, so the user only learned of the failure after separately navigating down the page. Screen reader and non-visual users cannot distinguish available from unavailable sizes before committing to a selection, causing a wasted, misleading step in the purchase flow.
interventions.mitigation: Expose the sold-out state programmatically wherever it is styled visually: set disabled (or aria-disabled="true" if the control must stay focusable for discoverability) on radio inputs inside size containers marked as sold out, and include the unavailability in the control's accessible name or label text (for example 'XS (Sold Out)') rather than relying on line-through styling alone. Additionally, announce the resulting availability/purchase-state change after a variant selection by placing the updated stock message in a live region (for example role="status") so it is conveyed without requiring manual re-navigation.

frictions.description: The homepage's main content has no heading elements and no landmark regions beyond a single footer, leaving hundreds of category links to traverse linearly (VO also reads the emoji before each subheading).

frictions.title: Category section titles lack heading semantics for VoiceOver navigation
frictions.description: VoiceOver heading navigation commands (VO+Shift+H) fail with 'Heading not found' because visual category section titles (community, services, housing, for sale, jobs) are structured as plain links without heading roles or tags (WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships).

interventions.description: Add ARIA heading roles to category section titles so VoiceOver heading navigation functions.

The category section titles on the area hub page (e.g. community, services, housing, for sale, jobs) are presented visually as section headers but are implemented as plain anchor elements with no heading element or role='heading'/aria-level in the DOM and accessibility tree. As a result, VoiceOver's heading navigation (VO+Shift+H) reported 'Heading not found' after five consecutive attempts, and the visual grouping structure of the page is not exposed programmatically. The observed consequence is that the user had no way to jump between the page's major sections and instead had to press Tab sequentially through a long list of individual category links (18 consecutive Tab presses observed in one segment) to reach content, making an already link-dense page slow and disorienting to traverse non-visually.
interventions.mitigation: Mark up each category section title with real heading semantics that match the visual hierarchy, for example wrapping or replacing the title link with an <h2> (or applying role='heading' with an appropriate aria-level when the element cannot be changed), while preserving the existing link target and focusability. Also consider grouping each category block in a landmark or section labelled by that heading so that structural navigation and rotor listing expose the same grouping users see visually.

The main category section titles on the Craigslist area homepage are rendered as links/text without HTML heading elements or role="heading", as confirmed in the page DOM and accessibility tree. blind.description: The banner contains an empty top-level heading (`<span role="heading" aria-level="1">` with no text) while the real page heading "Flight search" (class HeMQ4) is visually hidden, so heading-based navigation lands on a blank "heading level 1" and gives no orientation.

The ticket-type and cabin-class widgets are custom comboboxes whose `aria-controls` points at an empty `aria-hidden="true"` listbox (ids i9 / i22) while the real options live in a separate `ul`, and the combobox itself carries `aria-live="polite"`, producing wrong or duplicated announcements of the available/selected values.

The date-picker dialog renders several full month grids (July–October…) side by side in a fixed-width scrolling panel, forcing both horizontal and vertical scrolling once magnified.

frictions.description: The email signup popup modal overlays the page with a small close button ('X') at the top right, requiring repeated panning across the magnified viewport and extra zoom adjustments before successful activation.

interventions.description: Enlarge and highlight the promotional modal's close button for easier target acquisition under magnification.

An email signup modal overlays the storefront page with a small close button in its top-right corner. With screen magnification active, only a fraction of the viewport is visible at once, so the close control sits far from the user's current focus region. The recording shows the user clicking non-target areas of the modal, then re-adjusting magnification to locate and hit the small 'X' before the modal was dismissed. The only observed dismissal affordance is a small close control that was hard to locate and target while the person was using macOS System Zoom at high magnification, where only a fraction of the page is visible at any time. The person clicked in the backdrop area and attempted to activate the underlying 'SHOP NOW' hero button, both of which were blocked by the overlay, then zoomed out and back in to hunt for a dismissal control before abandoning the task and ending the session. Consequence: magnification users can be prevented from reaching primary shopping entry points at all, because the interruption is presented before any content interaction and its escape route is disproportionately small relative to the magnified viewport.
interventions.mitigation: Increase the close control's interactive target area to at least 44x44 CSS pixels (padding on the button rather than only a larger glyph), and give it a clearly visible boundary or background so it remains distinguishable against varying modal artwork. Position the close control predictably relative to the modal's own bounding box so it stays within view when the page is magnified, and ensure the modal is dismissible through additional low-precision routes such as the Escape key and an explicit 'No thanks' / 'Continue shopping' text button placed in the modal's normal reading flow. Consider deferring the promotional interruption until after a first user interaction or scroll so the landing view's primary calls to action are reachable without any dismissal step.

low_vision.description: The viewport meta declares `minimum-scale=1.0, maximum-scale=1.0`, disabling pinch-zoom so magnification users cannot scale this page's small product text and swatches on mobile.

frictions.title: Dynamic filter results update outside magnified viewport
frictions.description: Activating sidebar filters dynamically reloads search results outside the magnified view, forcing full-screen horizontal panning to locate updated content.

interventions.description: On the search results page (bestbuy.com/site/searchpage.jsp), activating a checkbox facet in the left sidebar (e.g. the "Outdoor" usage filter) triggers an asynchronous reload of the product grid. Because the grid sits far to the right of the sidebar, the update happens entirely outside the user's magnified viewport, and no perceivable confirmation appears near the control that was just activated. The observed consequence, repeated across three segments, was that the user had to pan the magnified view horizontally across the full page width to discover whether the filter had applied and what results remained (in this case a single sold-out refurbished Mini 2 listing). Each filter change therefore costs a full traversal of the layout, and the result count change is easy to miss entirely at high zoom.
interventions.mitigation: Announce and surface the result of filter changes in-context rather than only in the remote grid: expose the results container as a live region (e.g. aria-live="polite" on a concise status such as "12 results" / "1 result for Outdoor") so the change is programmatically communicated, and render an adjacent, visible confirmation next to the facet controls — for example an updated result count and applied-filter chips rendered within or immediately below the sidebar filter panel. Additionally, ensure the results region receives or can be reached without a long pointer traverse (for example, moving focus to the results heading after a filter is applied, or providing a "skip to results" mechanism), and verify the filtered results layout reflows so the sidebar and results are not separated by large horizontal distance at high zoom / narrow effective viewport widths.

interventions.description: Increase text contrast for main navigation links

interventions.description: Add a solid semi-opaque dark background behind header navigation menu links and banner text to maintain high contrast.

frictions.description: Under macOS Zoom magnification, moving the pointer across the viewport to inspect or reach menu options causes hover-revealed dropdowns ('Medical Care' and 'Prime') to prematurely dismiss, forcing repeated re-triggering (WCAG 1.4.13).

interventions.description: Header navigation menus on www.amazon.com reveal their dropdown content on pointer hover, but the hoverable region that keeps the dropdown open appears to be narrow and unforgiving. When the user magnifies the screen with macOS Zoom, pointer movement doubles as viewport panning, so small pointer travel needed to read the dropdown's contents repeatedly moved the pointer out of the trigger/popup area and the dropdown disappeared. Observed on the 'Medical Care' and 'Prime' menus across two segments (three occurrences). The consequence is that a magnified user cannot read or reach items in the dropdown without it vanishing mid-read, requiring repeated re-triggering and making the menu effectively unusable at high zoom levels.
interventions.mitigation: Make hover-revealed dropdowns persistent enough to be read and traversed under magnification: keep the popup visible while the pointer is anywhere over the trigger or the popup, include the intervening gap in the hoverable region (e.g. an invisible bridge area or padding), and add a dismissal delay (grace period) before hiding rather than hiding immediately on mouseleave. Also ensure the menus can be opened and kept open by click/keyboard activation and dismissed explicitly with Escape or by moving focus, so persistence does not depend on precise pointer positioning.

Key labels and previews are delivered only through hover-triggered `rpl-tooltip` (trigger="hover focus-visible") and `faceplate-hovercard` (`mouse-only`, 500ms enter / 150ms leave), transient content that a magnifier user cannot reliably hover, enlarge or dismiss.

so the level-1 heading is announced as a meaningless run-on string ("GmailSearchtabHelpTrainingSend feedback to GoogleUpgrade…Try Gemini"), and the page repeats identical hidden headings (three

Conversations

, two

Labels

Three near-identical mail toolbars (inbox, trash, spam variants) plus duplicated element ids used for naming (id="s" twice, id=":50" and id=":52" repeated in the tab panels) coexist in the DOM, so screen-reader users encounter multiple "Select", "Refresh", "More email options" and "inbox settings" controls with ambiguous or wrongly resolved accessible names.

low_vision.description: Per-message actions (archive, delete, mark as read, snooze) only render when the row is hovered (ul class="bqY" revealed on row hover), so magnified users who cannot see the whole row lose these controls and have no persistent equivalent.

Nearly all commands are unlabeled 20 px icon glyphs drawn from sprites/transparent spacers (images/cleardot.gif for star, pagination "Newer"/"Older", toolbar div class="asf"/"ar9" backgrounds), which become indistinguishable when enlarged or when background images are overridden by a custom stylesheet.

Unread status is signalled visually only by bold/darker styling (class "zF"/"bqe"/"bq3" versus "yP") with no visible text or icon, so low-vision users cannot reliably tell the unread "Study task email" from read messages.

The inbox uses an 11-column grid table plus fixed left navigation, sticky toolbars and a right side panel (role="complementary" "Side panel"), forcing two-dimensional scrolling of the message list at high zoom.

Secondary information is rendered in small light-grey text (snippet spans class="y2", timestamps, "0% of 15 GB used", "Last account activity: 0 minutes ago", icons filled #5F6368), which is hard to read for users needing higher contrast.

motor.description: Opening or triaging a message requires precise mouse clicks because rows, cells, checkboxes and the subject "link" are excluded from the tab order (tabindex="-1" or no tabindex on div role="link" class="xS"), leaving no standard keyboard path to the messages.

The row action buttons only exist while the pointer hovers the row (ul class="bqY" toolbar and the hover-revealed label arrow div class="pM aj0"), so users must hold a hover and then hit a small icon without drifting off the row — an unreliable transient interaction.

Many essential targets are tiny and tightly packed: the star cell (span class="aXw" over a spacer gif), the row checkbox, the 20 px toolbar icons, the tab-visibility button (div class="aKj") and the "Newer"/"Older" pagination arrows, all adjacent within a dense row.

Menu and chip controls fire on pointer-down/mouse-down (e.g. jsaction="pointerdown:FEiYhc", "mousedown:UX7yZ", "mousedown:p8EH2c" on the search-refinement buttons and dropdowns), so a tremor or mis-press activates them with no chance to move off and abort.
